question: Under the Inland Navigation Rules, what does a signal of two short blasts from a power-driven vessel indicate?
choice_a: Intent to alter course to port (or to pass on the other vessel's starboard side)
choice_b: Intent to overtake on the port side only
explanation: Under the Inland Navigation Rules, two short blasts signals an intent to alter course to port, the counterpart to the one-short-blast starboard-turn signal.
source_note: Universal Inland Navigation Rules maneuvering and warning signals (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: What does a signal of three short blasts indicate under the Inland Navigation Rules?
choice_a: The vessel is preparing to raise its anchor
choice_b: The vessel is operating astern propulsion (backing up)
choice_c: The vessel intends to overtake on the starboard side
choice_d: The vessel is requesting permission to cross a shipping channel
explanation: Three short blasts tells nearby vessels that a vessel is operating astern propulsion, meaning it is backing up, which is important information for anyone nearby judging its movement.
source_note: Universal Inland Navigation Rules maneuvering and warning signals (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: What does it mean for a vessel to be 'not under command' under the Navigation Rules, and how is it marked at night?
choice_a: It is a vessel that, through some exceptional circumstance such as mechanical failure, is unable to maneuver as required, shown at night by two all-round red lights in a vertical line
choice_b: It is any vessel operating without a licensed captain
choice_c: It refers only to a vessel that has run out of fuel while docked
choice_d: It is shown at night by a single green light
explanation: A vessel not under command cannot maneuver as the Rules require, typically due to an exceptional circumstance like mechanical failure, and displays two all-round red lights in a vertical line at night to warn other vessels to keep clear.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules vessel-not-under-command definition and lighting (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: During daylight, what day shapes does a vessel restricted in its ability to maneuver (such as one engaged in dredging) display?
choice_b: A vertical arrangement of a ball, diamond, and ball shape
choice_c: No shapes are ever required during daylight
explanation: A vessel restricted in its ability to maneuver displays a ball-diamond-ball day shape arrangement, signaling to nearby vessels that it has limited maneuvering ability and should be given a wide berth.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules day-shape requirements for restricted-maneuverability vessels (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: When two sailing vessels under sail alone are approaching each other and might collide, which vessel generally must keep clear?
choice_a: The vessel with the wind on its port side (port tack) must generally keep clear of a vessel with the wind on its starboard side (starboard tack)
choice_b: The larger sailboat always has right-of-way regardless of tack
choice_c: Whichever boat is moving faster has right-of-way
choice_d: Sailing vessels have no right-of-way rules between each other
explanation: Between two sailing vessels, the Navigation Rules generally require the vessel on port tack (wind coming over its port side) to keep clear of a vessel on starboard tack, among other tie-breaking rules for identical tacks or windward/leeward position.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules sailing-vessel-to-sailing-vessel right-of-way (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: How does the Navigation Rules' right-of-way hierarchy treat a vessel actively engaged in commercial fishing with nets or trawls that restrict its maneuverability, compared to an ordinary vessel underway?
choice_a: It has no special status and must always give way to recreational vessels
choice_b: It is treated similarly to other vessels restricted in their ability to maneuver, and other vessels should generally keep clear of it while its gear is deployed
choice_c: It is banned from operating in the same waters as recreational boats
choice_d: It automatically becomes the give-way vessel in every situation
explanation: A vessel actively engaged in fishing with gear such as trawls or nets that restricts its ability to maneuver is given special right-of-way consideration under the Rules, similar to other restricted-maneuverability vessels.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules right-of-way treatment of vessels engaged in fishing (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: In a narrow channel or fairway, what does the Navigation Rules require a vessel to do when it is safe and practicable?
choice_a: Travel down the exact center of the channel at all times
choice_b: Keep as near to the outer limit of the channel that lies on the vessel's own starboard side as is safe and practicable
choice_c: Keep to the port side of the channel
choice_d: There is no guidance for narrow channels
explanation: In a narrow channel or fairway, a vessel should keep as near to its own starboard-side outer limit as is safe and practicable, similar to keeping to the right side of a roadway, to keep the channel clear for oncoming and overtaking traffic.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules narrow-channel/fairway rule (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: Why should a boater generally avoid anchoring within a marked navigation channel on the Chesapeake Bay?
choice_a: Anchoring in a channel poses no risk to other vessels
choice_b: It is required practice whenever fuel runs low
choice_c: It can obstruct the passage of other vessels, including larger ships confined to the channel by their draft, except in a genuine emergency
choice_d: Channels are reserved exclusively for anchoring
explanation: Anchoring within a marked channel can block the passage of other vessels, particularly deep-draft ships that cannot leave the channel, so boaters should anchor outside channels except in a genuine emergency.
source_note: Chesapeake Bay commercial shipping channel navigation guidance, combined with universal Navigation Rules anchoring-in-channel caution
